strengths: Comprehensive and Well-Grounded Taxonomy: The paper proposes a structured 12-dimensional taxonomy that unifies composition (structured around scene graphs) and reasoning (structured around deductive, inductive, and abductive frameworks), offering a major step forward compared to heuristic benchmarks.

Focus on Real-World Complexity: Unlike existing benchmarks with low scene density or simple one-to-one reasoning, T2I-COREBENCH introduces high compositional density (~25 instances/attributes per prompt) and multi-step/causal reasoning chains, reflecting challenging real-world scenarios.

Rigorous Evaluation and Validation: The atomic checklist-based evaluation protocol (13,500 yes/no questions) is highly fine-grained. The authors conducted a robust human alignment study comparing multiple MLLMs with professional annotators, justifying the use of Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen2.5-VL as reliable evaluators.

Extensive Benchmarking: The paper evaluates a comprehensive suite of 27 current text-to-image models (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified models), revealing insightful trends, such as the trade-offs of integrating explicit reasoning ('thinking') before generation.
weaknesses: Evaluator Reliability on High-Density Scenes: Although the human alignment study shows reasonable agreement (~81% for Gemini 2.5 Flash), an error/disagreement rate of nearly 20% is still non-trivial. When models fail on complex tasks, it remains somewhat difficult to disentangle generator errors from MLLM evaluator hallucinations/omissions on very dense or cluttered images.

Confounding Prompt Length with Compositional Ability: The average prompt length of 170 tokens is exceptionally long. Many T2I models (particularly older or smaller ones) are heavily bottlenecked by text encoder context limits (e.g., CLIP's 77-token limit). The benchmark might inherently penalize models with weaker text encoders rather than those with weaker spatial/attribute binding capabilities per se.

Lack of Qualitative Failure Analysis: The paper is highly quantitative, but lacks visual examples of model generations showing where and how state-of-the-art models fail on these complex tasks. Visualizing a few case studies (e.g., of inductive or abductive reasoning failures) would significantly improve the clarity and educational value of the paper.

strengths: Comprehensive and principled taxonomy that unifies composition (scene-graph-based: instances, attributes, relations, text) and reasoning (philosophically grounded: deductive, inductive, abductive).
Adoption of a checklist-based evaluation protocol (around 13,500 atomic yes/no questions) which provides finer granularity and better interpretability than direct single-score MLLM grading.
Extensive experimental evaluation of 27 different T2I models, encompassing diverse architectures (diffusion, autoregressive, unified) and both open- and closed-source models.
Rigorous data construction pipeline employing three distinct state-of-the-art LRMs to prevent stylistic homogeneity, followed by strict multi-annotator human verification.
weaknesses: Incomplete manuscript details and placeholders: The paper contains noticeable unfinished elements, such as 'Our project page: .' on page 1 and the statement 'Additional experimental results... are actively being conducted in progress and will be included in the next version' on page 9. For a top-tier conference submission, these placeholders indicate a lack of polish and completeness.

Unjustified assumption in the human alignment study: The authors only evaluate human-to-MLLM alignment on the 4 compositional dimensions (MI, MA, MR, TR) and assume this is sufficient for the other 8 reasoning dimensions. Reasoning tasks (e.g., detecting implicit behavioral consequences, counterfactual physics, or abductive reasoning) are highly cognitive and potentially prone to different types of MLLM evaluator biases/hallucinations compared to simple existence checks of explicit scene graph elements.

Limited alignment with real-world user distribution: The prompts in the benchmark are extremely dense and complex (averaging 170 tokens). While this successfully tests the extreme capabilities of models, it does not represent typical user prompts, which may limit the benchmark's practical applicability for everyday T2I usage.
The paper is purely a benchmarking and evaluation study. While valuable, it lacks algorithmic or methodological novelty in terms of actual T2I model generation techniques.

strengths: Comprehensive and Well-Structured Taxonomy: The paper proposes a highly systematic 12-dimensional taxonomy covering both composition (instances, attributes, relations, text rendering) and reasoning (deductive, inductive, abductive), grounded in philosophical frameworks of inference.

Emphasis on High Complexity and Density: Unlike prior benchmarks that evaluate low-density scenes, T2I-COREBENCH focuses on semantically dense scenarios (~20 instances/attributes per prompt) and multi-step causal reasoning, presenting a more realistic and challenging evaluation for state-of-the-art models.

Fine-Grained Checklist-Based Protocol: Translating complex prompts into an atomic checklist of over 13,500 yes/no questions enables an objective, highly interpretable, and reproducible evaluation of T2I models.

Extensive Benchmarking: The paper evaluates an exceptionally wide range of 27 models, including leading open-source models (such as Flux and Qwen-Image) and closed-source commercial models (such as Imagen 4 Ultra and GPT-Image), which yields solid and insightful findings.
weaknesses: Potential Evaluation Bias from MLLM Evaluators: Although the authors conduct a valuable human alignment study to justify the choice of Gemini 2.5 Flash / Qwen2.5-VL-72B, MLLMs themselves struggle with dense attributes, precise spatial relations, and text rendering. These evaluator-side limitations could introduce systematic noise or false negatives in the evaluation results.

Implicit Expectations vs. Model Training: The 'reasoning' tasks require T2I models to deduce implicit visual states (e.g., chemical reactions, logical puzzles, or story progression). Since most T2I models are trained on highly descriptive text-image pairs rather than inference chains, the benchmark heavily penalizes the standard generation paradigm, which might reflect a mismatch in what modern T2I models are designed to do versus what they are evaluated on.

Data Generation Source Bias: Although human verification is applied in three rounds, using LRMs (Claude 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, o3) to construct the prompts and checklists might still introduce specific prompt-writing biases or linguistic patterns that favor certain models during evaluation.

strengths: Well-structured and theoretically grounded taxonomy: The paper unifies composition and reasoning into a 12-dimensional taxonomy, grounding reasoning in deductive, inductive, and abductive philosophical frameworks.

Comprehensive and extensive evaluation: The authors benchmark 38 text-to-image (T2I) models across different architectures (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified) and access types (open-source vs. closed-source), which is exceptionally thorough.

Fine-grained evaluation protocol: Instead of relying on problematic metrics like CLIPScore or direct holistic MLLM scoring, the paper constructs a massive dataset of 1,080 prompts paired with 13,536 human-verified, atomic yes/no questions.

Insightful analysis: The paper does not just present numbers; it offers valuable analysis, such as the systematic study of prompt rewriting (exploring native vs. augmented reasoning) and fine-grained analyses on POS vs. NEG constraints.
High-quality writing and presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, clearly illustrated, and includes rich qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dependency on MLLM evaluators: Although the authors provide human-alignment verification showing ~81% balanced accuracy, the remaining gap indicates that MLLM evaluations (like Gemini 2.5 Flash) still carry some noise that could affect the evaluation of closely performing models.

Potential LRM generation bias: While generating prompts using three diverse LRMs (Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI o3) mitigates bias, T2I models that share similar text encoders or training histories with these LRMs might still receive an unfair advantage.

Departure from typical user prompts: With an average prompt length of 170 tokens and ~25 instances per prompt, the benchmark represents extremely dense and complex edge cases rather than typical user behavior, which might limit its relevance to standard text-to-image application scenarios.

strengths: A highly comprehensive and structured taxonomy: T2I-CoReBench evaluates text-to-image models across 12 distinct dimensions, elegantly dividing them into composition (using scene graph elements: instance, attribute, relation, text) and reasoning (using a tripartite philosophical framework: deductive, inductive, abductive).

Increased complexity and density: Unlike prior benchmarks that focus on simple scenarios, this benchmark features high compositional density (averaging ~20 elements per prompt) and multi-step reasoning chains (e.g., one-to-many and many-to-one inferences), pushing the limits of modern T2I models.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors benchmark 38 current open-source and closed-source T2I models across different architectures (diffusion, autoregressive, unified). The inclusion of up-to-date models like Flux.2 and GPT-Image-1.5 provides valuable insights into the current state of the art.

Reliable, fine-grained evaluation protocol: Using a checklist of atomic binary yes/no questions (amounting to 13,500 questions) avoids holistic grading errors. The authors also validate their MLLM-based evaluator against human annotations, demonstrating strong alignment.

Insightful analysis on prompt rewriting: The paper demonstrates that while prompt rewriting significantly boosts weaker models, it fails to solve core multimodal reasoning issues (such as overriding strong visual priors like 'circular wheels' to make them square), highlighting future research directions.
weaknesses: Potential stylistic bias from LLM-generated prompts: Although the authors utilize three different state-of-the-art LRMs (Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI o3) to mitigate bias, the prompts are ultimately model-generated and might not fully reflect the natural variety, phrasing, or errors of human-written prompts.

Limitations of MLLM evaluators: While Table 5 shows reasonable human alignment (balanced accuracy around 70-80% for top-performing MLLMs), MLLMs still occasionally struggle with highly detailed spatial relationships, precise counting, and fine-grained text rendering layout, which could introduce minor noise into the automatic scoring.

Scope constraints: As noted in the limitations, the benchmark is currently restricted to English prompts, lacks evaluations of aesthetic quality or image realism, and focuses primarily on objects and animals rather than complex human-centric or face-centric actions.

strengths: Well-motivated and theoretically grounded taxonomy: The 12 evaluation dimensions are cleanly mapped to scene-graph components (for composition) and classical logical frameworks (deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning).

Push for realistic complexity: By scaling up compositional density (~25 elements) and reasoning depth (multi-step, many-to-one, and one-to-many inferences), the benchmark avoids performance saturation and clearly differentiates top-tier models.

Robust evaluation protocol: The combination of Large Reasoning Model (LRM) generation, rigorous multi-round human verification by experts, and atomic MLLM-based checklist evaluation ensures high reproducibility and reliable metrics.

Comprehensive benchmarking: Evaluating 38 models across diverse architectures (diffusion, autoregressive, and unified models) and access modes (open-source and closed-source) provides a clear and valuable snapshot of the current state of the art.

Insightful analyses: The investigations into the impact of prompt rewriting, positive vs. negative constraints, and logical multi-hop scaling provide deep, actionable findings for future text-to-image (T2I) model development.
weaknesses: Evaluator model dependency: The evaluation pipeline relies on Gemini 2.5 Flash acting as the visual auditor. Although the authors present a helpful human alignment study, MLLMs can still exhibit systematic errors in complex counting, spatial relationships, or fine-grained OCR, which may introduce minor bias.

Unnatural prompt style: To enforce high semantic density, many prompts read like highly detailed paragraphs or instruction lists rather than natural, colloquial user queries, which might not fully align with typical downstream user distributions.

Cost of evaluation: Running over 13,500 visual QA checks per model makes evaluation computationally heavy and potentially costly if commercial APIs are utilized, which may hinder its use as a lightweight validation suite during active development.
